paras: The lynching of Jack Jones was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at or near Rockwood, Tennessee, reported as having taken place on Thursday, November 22, 1888. Jones was accused of assaulting, or attempting to assault, two women who lived near Rockwood. The story travelled only as one-sentence telegraph and column items, which ran in papers from New York and New Jersey to Mississippi and Louisiana over the following week.

According to the fullest account, a 'Southern Gleanings' paragraph, Jones was 'a negro hailing from Macon, Ga.' That paragraph named the two women as Mrs. John Haggard and Miss Hedgroth and said they lived near Rockwood. The New York Sun gave the second name as Miss Hedgecath and added that the women had fed him before the alleged assault.

The accounts describe the alleged offense differently: the Camden Evening Telegram said Jones had assaulted 'a white woman', while other papers said he 'attempted to criminally assault two women' or made 'an unsuccessful criminal assault' on them. In the Sun's version, a crowd of angry men pursued and captured him. The Camden paper reported that he 'was hanged by a mob in Rockwood, Tenn., Thursday', and the column paragraphs said he 'was caught by an angry mob and lynched.'
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and no member of the mob is named.

Northern papers handled the case as a line of news digest. On November 23 the New York Evening World's 'News Summary' reported that 'Two negroes are lynched, one in Tennessee and the other in Louisiana, for assaulting white women', without naming either man, and the Camden Evening Telegram listed the Rockwood hanging among its 'Telegraphic Brevities.' The next day the Sun ran its own item among 'Sparks from the Telegraph.'

Two syndicated paragraphs carried the story to Southern and Midwestern weeklies. The 'Pointed Paragraphs' version appeared in the Maysville Evening Bulletin and the Clarksville Evening Chronicle on November 24, in the Stanford Semi-Weekly Interior Journal on November 27, and in the Napoleon, Ohio, Democratic Northwest on November 29. The 'Southern Gleanings' version ran in the Oxford Eagle on November 29, the Bolivar Bulletin on November 30, and the Huntsville Gazette and St. Landry Democrat on December 1. Every version stated the alleged assault as fact and reported the lynching without comment, set among items on fires, accidents and crimes.

The Sun's item, which called the man John Jones and placed the alleged assault at King's Creek, Tennessee, said only that 'It is more than probable that they hanged him.' The Camden brief and both syndicated paragraphs stated without qualification that he had been hanged or lynched, and the same two women's names tie the Sun's item to the Rockwood case. The papers also differ on whether one woman or two were involved, with the Camden brief alone giving one.

reader.title: Lynching of Jack Jones
bases: Jack Jones was reported hanged or lynched by a mob after being accused of assaulting women near Rockwood, Tenn. (A3, A4, A8).

Three separate briefs say a mob hanged or lynched Jones for an alleged assault on women (A3, A4, A8); the Sun's earlier telegraph item said only that it was 'more than probable' that the crowd of angry men who captured him hanged him (A6).

The Camden telegraphic brief (A3), the 'Pointed Paragraphs' brief (A4) and the 'Southern Gleanings' paragraph (A8) differ in wording and detail but agree that a mob lynched Jack Jones near Rockwood for an alleged assault; the Sun (A6) hedged on the outcome but did not deny it.

accounts.label: Telegraphic brief (Camden Evening Telegram)
accounts.gist: Jack Jones, 'a colored man', was hanged by a mob in Rockwood on Thursday for assaulting a white woman.

accounts.label: Wire paragraph ('Pointed Paragraphs')
accounts.gist: Jones attempted to assault two women near Rockwood and was caught by an angry mob and lynched.

accounts.label: Sun telegraph item
accounts.gist: John Jones assaulted Mrs. John Haggard and Miss Hedgecath at King's Creek after they had fed him, and was pursued and captured by angry men who, the Sun said, more than probably hanged him.

accounts.label: 'Southern Gleanings' column
accounts.gist: Jones, from Macon, Ga., made an unsuccessful assault on Mrs. Haggard and Miss Hedgroth near Rockwood a few nights earlier and was caught by an angry mob and lynched.

framing.detail: Northern papers ran the story as one line in summary columns ('News Summary', 'Telegraphic Brevities', 'Sparks from the Telegraph'), stating the accusation as fact without comment.
Southern and border papers carried it in the 'Southern Gleanings' and 'Pointed Paragraphs' columns, again presenting the alleged assault as fact.

versions.value: captured by a crowd; 'more than probable that they hanged him'

conflicts.note: The Sun's hedged item is consistent with an early report written before the hanging was confirmed; the other three accounts state the killing flatly.
Same surname and the same two women make it the same episode.
The Gleanings paragraph says the women lived near Rockwood; King's Creek may be the locality near Rockwood, but the papers do not say so.
Three accounts, two of which name the women, say two.

record_check.record: Brief item ... No date, victim name or local detail is given for this Tennessee case.
record_check.dossier: Other papers name the victim (Jack Jones, or John Jones), the place (Rockwood, or King's Creek), the day (Thursday, 22 Nov.), the two women (Mrs. John Haggard and Miss Hedgroth/Hedgecath) and his origin (Macon, Ga.).
Accused of assaulting a white woman (one paper) or attempting to assault two women (three papers); only the Camden and New York summary items state the women's race.
in_pursuit: pursued and captured by a crowd of angry men.
No paper names the county; papers give only Rockwood (or King's Creek), Tenn.
The alleged assault on women was the stated reason for the lynching.

info: Thursday, 22 November 1888 (the Camden brief of 23 November says the hanging took place 'Thursday'); the Gleanings paragraph says the assault was alleged 'a few nights ago'
Rockwood, Tenn. (A3), or near Rockwood (A4, A8); the Sun places the alleged assault at King's Creek, Tenn. (A6)
Jack Jones, described as 'a colored man' (A3) and 'a negro' (A4, A8), 'hailing from Macon, Ga.' (A8); the Sun calls him John Jones (A6)

Accused of assaulting a white woman (A3), of attempting to assault two women (A4), or of an 'unsuccessful criminal assault' on Mrs. John Haggard and Miss Hedgroth (A8; 'Hedgecath' in A6), after the women had fed him (A6)
'a mob' (A3); 'an angry mob' (A4, A8); 'a crowd of angry men' (A6); no one is named
